name: South America

fields.description:
South America stretches from the Caribbean coasts of Colombia and Venezuela to Tierra del Fuego, with the Andes running down the Pacific side and the Amazon basin filling the north and centre. Twelve sovereign countries share it, mostly Spanish-speaking, with Portuguese in Brazil. For a traveller, altitude and distance shape a trip more than borders do.

## Overview

The continent is bounded by the Pacific to the west, the Atlantic to the east and the Caribbean Sea to the north, and ends at the Tierra del Fuego archipelago, divided between Chile and Argentina. The Andes run for roughly 7,000 km down the western side through Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina; Aconcagua in Argentina is the highest summit. East of the range the Amazon basin covers much of Brazil and reaches into Peru, Colombia and Bolivia, the Orinoco drains Venezuela, and the Paraná, Paraguay and Uruguay rivers meet at the Río de la Plata between Buenos Aires and Montevideo. Useful subregions are the Caribbean north (Colombia, Venezuela and the Guianas), the Andean countries (Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia), the Southern Cone (Chile, Argentina, Uruguay, Paraguay) and Brazil, which takes up most of the east. The Atacama Desert in northern Chile and Patagonia in the far south are separated by thousands of kilometres.

## History and Ancient Civilizations

Many visitors follow the Inca. Cusco in Peru was the capital of their empire, and Machu Picchu and the Sacred Valley lie nearby. Older sites include Caral in Peru, a Norte Chico city more than 4,000 years old, the Nazca Lines on Peru's southern coast, and Tiwanaku in Bolivia, close to Lake Titicaca. Spanish rule left walled and fortified towns such as Cartagena in Colombia, the historic centre of Quito in Ecuador, Colonia del Sacramento in Uruguay and the silver city of Potosí in Bolivia. Portuguese Brazil is represented by gold-era Ouro Preto. The Jesuit missions of the Guaraní survive as ruins at San Ignacio Miní in Argentina and São Miguel das Missões in Brazil. Most countries won independence in the 1810s and 1820s, and Simón Bolívar's campaigns are commemorated in plazas and museums across the northern Andes.

## Getting around South America

The main international hubs are São Paulo-Guarulhos (GRU), Bogotá El Dorado (BOG), Lima Jorge Chávez (LIM), Santiago Arturo Merino Benítez (SCL) and Buenos Aires Ezeiza (EZE), with Quito (UIO) as a further Andean gateway. There is no continent-wide rail network, so most crossings are by air or long-distance coach; Sky Airline and JetSMART run low-cost routes among Chile, Peru, Argentina and neighbours. Rail is mainly scenic: PeruRail connects Cusco with Machu Picchu and Puno. Ferries cross the Río de la Plata from Buenos Aires to Colonia del Sacramento and Montevideo, and a boat-and-bus route links Bariloche in Argentina with Puerto Varas in Chile. Peru and Bolivia meet by road at Lake Titicaca. Flying is necessary for the Amazon interior, Patagonia from the north, and routes such as Bogotá to Buenos Aires.

## When to visit South America

Seasons depend on subregion and altitude. In the Andean highlands around Cusco, La Paz and Quito the dry season runs roughly May to September, with sunny days near 20°C in Cusco and nights close to freezing in June and July; rain is heaviest from December to March, which also brings the wet season on the Bolivian altiplano. The Amazon stays hot at around 25–32°C year-round, with heavier rain from about December to May. The Southern Cone has a December–February summer: Buenos Aires and Santiago reach around 30°C, and Patagonia is most accessible from November to March, when days are mild and winds strong. Winter closes many Patagonian services. The Caribbean coast of Colombia is driest from December to March. Peaks to plan around include Carnival in February or March, Semana Santa in March or April, Inti Raymi in Cusco on 24 June, Peru's national holidays in late July, Chile's on 18 September, and Christmas and New Year.

## Travel Notes

No single currency covers the continent. Ecuador uses the US dollar; most others have their own, including the Brazilian real, Peruvian sol, Colombian, Chilean, Argentine and Uruguayan pesos, and the Bolivian boliviano. Plug types differ: Brazil uses types N and C, Argentina I and C, Chile C and L, Peru A, B and C, and Colombia A and B, so carry an adaptor set. Spanish is the working language in most countries, Portuguese in Brazil, English in Guyana, Dutch in Suriname and French in French Guiana; Quechua, Aymara and Guaraní are widely spoken locally. Traffic drives on the right except in Guyana and Suriname, where it keeps left.

## Interesting Facts About South America

- The Andes stretch about 7,000 km, the longest continental mountain range.
- Aconcagua, in Argentina, is the highest mountain outside Asia.
- Chile and Ecuador are the only countries that do not border Brazil.
- Lake Titicaca is shared by Peru and Bolivia, at roughly 3,800 metres.
- The equator crosses Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil, and gives Ecuador its name.
fields.tldr: Fly into São Paulo, Bogotá, Lima, Santiago or Buenos Aires and expect to fly again: distances are huge and no continental rail network exists. Coaches, ferries and low-cost airlines link neighbours. Go to the Andes May–September, Patagonia November–March, and allow for Carnival and holiday peaks.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit South America?
faqs.a: It depends on where you go. The Andean highlands are driest from about May to September, Patagonia is best from November to March, and the Amazon is hot all year with heavier rain from roughly December to May.

faqs.q: How many countries are in South America?
faqs.a: There are 12 sovereign countries: Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, Paraguay, Peru, Suriname, Uruguay and Venezuela. French Guiana is an overseas territory of France, and the Falkland Islands are a British overseas territory.

faqs.q: Do I need to fly between countries in South America?
faqs.a: Often, yes. There is no continent-wide rail network, and long coach journeys cross Andean passes. Neighbouring cities can be linked by coach or ferry, such as Buenos Aires to Montevideo, but the Amazon, Patagonia and long north–south legs usually need flights.

faqs.q: Which airports are the main hubs in South America?
faqs.a: São Paulo-Guarulhos (GRU), Bogotá (BOG), Lima (LIM), Santiago (SCL) and Buenos Aires Ezeiza (EZE) are the main international gateways, with Quito (UIO) serving the northern Andes. Many onward connections run through one of these.

faqs.q: Which language should I learn for South America?
faqs.a: Spanish is the most useful, as it is spoken in most countries. Brazil uses Portuguese. English is official in Guyana, Dutch in Suriname and French in French Guiana.

faqs.q: Is altitude a concern when travelling in the Andes?
faqs.a: Yes. Cusco is at around 3,400 metres and La Paz is higher, so many travellers feel breathless on arrival. Plan a slow first day, and check with a doctor beforehand if you have a health condition.

previous.description:
South America is a continent of dramatic contrasts — the world's largest rainforest, its driest desert, its longest mountain chain, and river systems that drain nearly half the landmass, all shared across 12 sovereign nations and roughly 440 million people.

## Overview

South America occupies roughly 17.8 million km² in the Western Hemisphere, tapering from the broad tropical north to the narrow, wind-scoured tip of Patagonia. The Andes run the full length of the western edge — one of the world's longest and highest mountain chains — while the Amazon Basin dominates the interior with the planet's largest tropical rainforest. The continent comprises 12 independent countries. Spanish is the dominant language across nine of them; Portuguese is the primary language of Brazil, which alone accounts for nearly half the continent's land area and population. Indigenous languages — including Quechua and Guaraní — retain official status or wide use in several countries. Culturally, the continent reflects layered Indigenous, Iberian, African, and later European and Asian immigrant influences.

## History and Ancient Civilizations

Human presence in South America dates back at least 14,000 years. The most architecturally visible pre-Columbian civilization is the Inca Empire, which by the early 16th century stretched from present-day Colombia to central Chile and left enduring sites including Machu Picchu and the sacred city of Cusco. Earlier cultures — among them the Tiwanaku and Wari — shaped the Andean highlands centuries before. Spanish and Portuguese colonization began in earnest after 1492, restructuring the political map entirely over two centuries. Most nations achieved independence in the early 19th century, largely between 1810 and 1825. UNESCO World Heritage Sites across the continent — including the historic centre of Quito, the Jesuit missions of the Guaraní, and the Nazca Lines — preserve multiple layers of that history.

## Travel Notes

Visa requirements vary considerably: many South American countries offer visa-free entry to European and North American passport holders, though Venezuela and others impose restrictions. Climate zones range from equatorial (year-round humidity in the Amazon) to Mediterranean (central Chile), so no single travel season applies continent-wide. The Southern Cone's summer runs November–March. Currencies are entirely fragmented — no regional single currency exists. Regional aviation connects major hubs including São Paulo, Bogotá, Lima, and Buenos Aires; overland distances are vast.

## Interesting Facts About South America

- Amazon River carries the most water.
- Andes form Earth's longest mountain chain.
- Atacama is the driest nonpolar desert.
- Brazil is the largest country.
- Lake Titicaca sits at high altitude.
